finding.claim: The /settings/email POST endpoint uses @login_optional instead of @login_required, so unauthenticated requests reach set_email with g.uid=None. This is a missing authentication check on a state-changing account operation. If set_email treats a None uid as a wildcard or a real record, an anonymous caller could change or take over account email addresses, which can lead to account takeover through password reset. Even if it only no-ops, the auth control is missing and inconsistent with /settings/password.
finding.source: Any unauthenticated HTTP client sending POST /settings/email with no session cookie
finding.sink: set_email(g.uid, ...) at routes.py:37, an account email modification

trace.note: login_optional sets g.uid = session.get('uid'), which is None when anonymous, and never aborts
set_email(g.uid, ...) is called with uid None

finding.guards_checked: login_required (lines 8-16) would abort(401) but is not applied here. There is no other auth check in the handler, no CSRF protection, and no before_request hook. set_email is a stub (line 48), so the impact depends on its real implementation.

verdict.guard_found: none (login_required at routes.py:8-16 aborts 401 but is not applied to change_email; login_optional at routes.py:19-25 never aborts)
verdict.reason: routes.py:35 applies @login_optional, which sets g.uid=None without aborting (routes.py:22), so an anonymous POST reaches set_email(None, ...) at routes.py:37 with no other guard. The stub at routes.py:48 means the account-takeover impact is unproven, but the missing authentication check is real.
